messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Ragged array spec
parts:
Thanks. That's super helpful.

The other question is whether we want ragged arrays defined
the same way. The problem here is how we define

real a[rows,cols,shelves];

since they're nested. I'm still pondering this.

But we could definitely start with arrays of differently sized
matrices.

How would you feel about using just matrix[rows,cols] instead
of "ragged_matrix"? I really don't like "ragged_matrix", because
the matrix isn't itself ragged.

Also, I'd strongly prefer

vector[cols] beta[K];

to

ragged_matrix[cols,rep_array(1,K)] beta[K];

I don't think we want to get in the habit of defining N x 1
or 1 x N matrices since they'll behave like matrices, not
like vectors. And I absolutely don't want to coerce one into
the other automatically.

I'm not sure about doing all these random effects things only
by indexing rather than by name. But your mileage may vary. And
I see the problem with big ones either way --- with arrays you
have to keep some kind of symbol table mapping from indexes to
names, whereas with names, you have what looks like duplicated code.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Ragged array spec
parts:
On Tuesday, March 31, 2015 at 7:40:07 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The other question is whether we want ragged arrays defined
the same way.  The problem here is how we define

  real a[rows,cols,shelves];

since they're nested.  I'm still pondering this.

Good point. But for homogenously sized arrays of matrices currently
matrix[rows,cols] X[shelves]
it is accessed by shelf, row, and column. That is confusing, but we should be consistenly confusing.

How would you feel about using just matrix[rows,cols] instead
of "ragged_matrix"?  I really don't like "ragged_matrix", because
the matrix isn't itself ragged.
Agree. A matrix is a matrix.

Also, I'd strongly prefer

  vector[cols] beta[K];

to

  ragged_matrix[cols,rep_array(1,K)] beta[K];
Also agree.

I'm not sure about doing all these random effects things only
by indexing rather than by name.  But your mileage may vary.  And
I see the problem with big ones either way --- with arrays you
have to keep some kind of symbol table mapping from indexes to
names, whereas with names, you have what looks like duplicated code.

Part of the reason for doing this is to auto-generate Stan code or to use Stan code that can be compiled once at install time. We can figure out the naming on the (R for the near term) interface side but we need to be able to write abstract code on the Stan side.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Ragged array spec
parts:
On Tuesday, March 31, 2015 at 8:08:43 PM UTC-4, robert.trangucci wrote:
Right now my plan is to handle naming in RStan rather than in the Stan code. I believe there's a way to specify names in the print function. The more general the Stan code, the less often it'll need to be compiled.

You can just specify

names(stanfit) <- big_character_vector

and it is supposed to then work with every post-estimation command. We'll do that internally in rstanarm functions so that the output looks like that of the estimator it is emulating.

Ben

problemw ith the

> On Apr 1, 2015, at 1:23 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, March 31, 2015 at 10:10:09 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The other issue is I/O. What is the right data structure to use
> from R? We'll have to update the data and inits parser.
>
> I think either a list of matrices or possibly a long vector whose length is equal to the number of elements.

The list of matrices isn't general enough. It might be 3D, as in

{
{
{ 1 },
{ 2, 3}
},
{
{ 4, 5, 6}
}
}

And it might involve integers and not real values.

Simple vectors are compact, but they don't include sizing
information, so there's no error checking.

I'm thinking in terms of what users specify when they say things like

data=list(sigma=0.3, beta=c(1,2,3), ...)

The only solution I see now that I think about it is lists all
the way down, as in

foo=list(list(c(1), c(2,3)), list(c(4,5,6)))

That is,

> list(list(c(1), c(2,3)), list(c(4,5,6)))
[[1]]
[[1]][[1]]
[1] 1

[[1]][[2]]
[1] 2 3


[[2]]
[[2]][[1]]
[1] 4 5 6


- Bob
